You are a talented web engineer and technical marketing designer who has shipped high-polish product landing pages for developer tools. You've been handed a design document and asked to put together a plan to build what it describes. You will not be able to talk to the person who wrote it. This is a READ-ONLY review — do not write any files.

The project repo is at /home/alexa/repos/agentic-odi — you may read files there to ground your review (README.md, pyproject.toml, mcp_server/, client/).

Here is the design document:

---
# Design: agentic-odi GitHub Pages marketing site

## Intent & Why
Ship a customer-facing GitHub Pages site for agentic-odi (an experimental MCP-based testbed for Outcome-Driven Innovation). Audience: product managers, innovation teams, and AI/agent developers. The site answers why/what/how/when with a Jobsian sensibility: one page, ruthless focus, empathy for the user's pain, craft in typography and motion, no jargon soup, one obvious CTA. The bar: what a principal CTO under Steve Jobs would ship.

## Goals
- One scrollable landing page that converts a curious PM/eng lead into trying the hosted demo or cloning the repo.
- Communicate the core insight: "stop shipping guesses; ground agents in verified customer outcomes."
- Feel state-of-the-art: fast, accessible, beautiful type, subtle tasteful motion, dark-mode-aware, perfect on mobile.
- Deploy automatically to GitHub Pages on push to main via GitHub Actions.

## Non-Goals / Anti-Goals
- NOT a docs site (no MkDocs/Docusaurus), no blog, no nav maze.
- NOT claiming OSS license (repo has none — all rights reserved) or overstating maturity (site must carry honest "experimental" framing).
- NOT a framework-heavy build: no React/Next/Astro. Hand-crafted static HTML + CSS + minimal vanilla JS. Zero runtime deps, Lighthouse 95+.

## Constraints
- Source lives in `website/` at repo root (`docs/` is reserved for internal specs; `/site` is gitignored so use a different output path or force-add strategy — prefer keeping sources directly deployable, i.e., Pages serves `website/` contents via actions/upload-pages-artifact).
- Deploy workflow: `.github/workflows/pages.yml` using actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages; triggers on push to main paths `website/**` and the workflow itself.
- No visual assets exist in repo. Site must include: hand-designed minimal SVG wordmark ("agentic odi" + simple geometric mark), favicon (SVG), OG/Twitter card image (1200×630 — generate as static SVG or HTML-drawn; note OG images on Pages need a real raster ideally — plan an SVG for favicon/inline and either a committed PNG generated by a tiny script or an SVG OG fallback).
- Copy honesty: cite the ODI ~86% success-rate claim carefully ("as reported by Strategyn/ODI literature"), frame product as experimental, hosted endpoint requires auth.
- Fonts: system font stack (-apple-system / SF Pro on Apple, Segoe, etc.) — no webfont downloads; typographic craft via weight/tracking/scale.
- Dark/light via prefers-color-scheme.
- Accessibility: semantic landmarks, contrast AA+, reduced-motion respect.

## Page structure (Jobsian narrative)
1. Hero: the enemy = the guess. Headline direction: "Your roadmap is a guess." Sub: one sentence on grounding AI agents in verified customer outcomes. Single CTA (Try the hosted demo) + secondary (View on GitHub).
2. The Problem: shipping features nobody needs; the cost of opinion-driven development. Short, punchy, maybe a 3-beat parallel structure.
3. The Insight: what ODI/JTBD is in ~3 plain sentences + the outcome-satisfaction/opportunity-score idea visualized simply (e.g., a small CSS/SVG quadrant or bar showing Opportunity = Importance − Satisfaction). Stat callout with citation caveat.
4. How it works: 3 steps — capture jobs & outcomes in the MCP server; agents query the outcome database (MCP tools); PMs steer in The Living Studio. Small code/terminal snippet for the MCP endpoint. Screenshot placeholder for Living Studio (no screenshots exist — plan a tasteful illustrative SVG/CSS mock of the UI rather than a fake screenshot).
5. For builders: MCP endpoint, install one-liner (uv sync --all-packages; python -m client.run), links to repo.
6. Honest status: experimental badge, what works today, roadmap framing (when).
7. Footer: copyright (no license), links, "Built with outcomes, not guesses."

## What's left to the builder
Exact CSS scale/spacing system, exact copy micro-polish, SVG mark design details, animation choreography choices, workflow YAML specifics.
---
Report ONLY the questions you'd still need answered before you could plan this well: places where you'd have to guess and a wrong guess would matter. For each, give the question and why the answer changes the plan. Rank them by importance. Skip anything the document explicitly leaves to the builder, and anything you could reasonably decide yourself. Skip nitpicks about wording. If nothing important is left, say "nothing important left".

16: 17: --- 18: 19: ## 📋 Table of Contents 20: 21: - [The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation](#-the-vision-context-aware-innovation) 22: - [Current State (Experimental Testbed)](#-current-state-experimental-testbed) 23: - [Code Overview](#-code-overview) 24: - [Getting Started](#-getting-started) 25: - [Command-Line Interface (CLI)](#-command-line-interface-cli) 26: - [Manage Customer Outcomes](#-manage-customer-outcomes) 27: - [External Connectors (MCP Ingest)](#-external-connectors-mcp-ingest) 28: - [One-Command Launch](#-one-command-launch-recommended) 29: - [Manual Split-Terminal](#-manual-split-terminal-alternative) 30: - [Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend](#-local-tools-capable-llm-backend-for-mcp-testing) 31: - [Agent-Driven Testing](#-agent-driven-testing) 32: - [Linting, Formatting & Type Checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) 33: - [Testing](#-testing) 34: - [Test Coverage Map](#-test-coverage-map) 35: - [Agent Session Tracking](#-agent-session-tracking) 36: - [Superpowers with Pi](#-superpowers-with-pi) 37: - [Developer Workflow for Formatting](#-developer-workflow-for-formatting) 38: - [Deployment](#-deployment) 39: - [Roadmap & Next Steps](#-roadmap--next-steps) 40: - [Contributing](#-contributing) 41: - [License](#-license) 42: 43: --- 44: 45: ## 🌟 The Vision: Context-Aware Innovation 46: 47: **Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)**, built on the "Jobs-to-be-Done" theory, relies on deeply understanding customer needs, desired outcomes, and execution contexts. Historically, applying ODI requires meticulous research, structured data modeling, and rigorous analysis. 48: 49: **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** represents a paradigm shift in how AI systems consume and reason over external context. By adopting MCP, we can bridge the gap between static user research and dynamic, agentic AI. 50: 51: The vision for **Agentic ODI** is to build a unified, open protocol where LLMs and autonomous agents can natively query, understand, and reason over ODI data (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and Opportunity Scores) dynamically in real-time. Instead of feeding LLMs disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server will act as the "brain" of customer needs, allowing agents to invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions strictly anchored in verified user outcomes. 52: 53: --- 54: 55: ## 🏗️ Current State (Experimental Testbed) 56: 57: This repository serves as an initial sandbox for understanding server-client MCP communication streams. We are utilizing [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) to prototype HTTP-based context delivery. 58: 59: --- 60: 61: ## 🧩 Code Overview 62: 63: This repository is a [uv workspace](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/workspaces/) made up of **six** installable projects, each with its own `pyproject.toml`, `src/` layout, and tests: 64: 65: | Package | Description | 66: |---|---| 67: | **`core/`** (`agentic-odi-core`) | Domain models, the `ODIService` business-logic layer, and repository implementations (in-memory and SQLite), including ODI opportunity-score computation. | 68: | **`mcp_server/`** (`agentic-odi-mcp-server`) | A foundational MCP Server exposing an HTTP transport layer. It hosts tools for Jobs, Steps, Desired Outcomes, and Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value). | 69: | **`local_server/`** (`agentic-odi-local-server`) | A local FastAPI server that talks to the repository directly (no MCP transport). | 70: | **`client/`** (`agentic-odi-client`) | **The Living Studio** — a spatial, conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation. Provides an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous conversational agent connected to the MCP server. It also hosts `run.py`, the local dev launcher that starts the server and the Studio UI together. | 71: | **`cli/`** (`agentic-odi-cli`) | A [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based command-line interface. It provides version/help plus `outcomes` and `connectors` commands. | 72: | **`connectors/`** (`agentic-odi-connectors`) | Pluggable external integrations. The first kind is an **MCP client connector** that connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP, checks health, and ingests tools/resources into a local ingest sink. Additional kinds (REST, webhooks, and so on) can register against the same protocol later. | 73: 74: --- 75: 76: ## 🚀 Getting Started 77: 78: ### Prerequisites 79: 80: - **Python** 3.10+ 81: - [**uv**](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager 82: 83: Install the entire workspace (all six projects plus dev tooling): 84: 85: ```bash 86: uv sync --all-packages 87: ``` 88: 89: This creates a `.venv` and installs `agentic-odi-core`, `agentic-odi-mcp-server`, `agentic-odi-local-server`, `agentic-odi-client`, `agentic-odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi-connectors` in editable mode. 90: 91: ### 💻 Command-Line Interface (CLI) 92: 93: The [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based CLI lets you interact with Agentic ODI directly from your terminal — no chat UI required. It provides version and help information plus commands for connecting to external systems. Over time it will also expose commands for working with the ODI dataset (Jobs, Steps, and Outcomes). 94: 95: Launch it with: 96: 97: ```bash 98: python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version 99: python -m cli --help # show available options and commands 100: python -m cli # show help when no command is given 101: ``` 102: 103: A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. 104: 105: ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes 106: 107: Manage Customer Outcomes (linking customer value to business value) via the CLI. The CLI acts as an MCP client, so the server must be running (`python -m mcp_server`): 108: 109: ```bash 110: # Add a Customer Outcome 111: agentic-odi outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" 112: 113: # List outcomes (optionally filtered) 114: agentic-odi outcomes list 115: agentic-odi outcomes list --job-id 116: 117: # Get, update, delete 118: agentic-odi outcomes get 119: agentic-odi outcomes update --importance 9.0 120: agentic-odi outcomes delete --yes 121: 122: # Compute ODI Opportunity Score 123: agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 124: ``` 125: 126: Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` to point to a non-default server if needed. 127: 128: ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) 129: 130: Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. 131: 132: ```bash 133: python -m cli connectors add mcp --name gong --url http://localhost:9000/mcp --tool latest_quote 134: python -m cli connectors list 135: python -m cli connectors health --name gong 136: python -m cli connectors ingest --name gong 137: ``` 138: 139: Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. 140: 141: ### ⚡ One-Command Launch (recommended) 142: 143: `python -m client.run` starts both the MCP server and the Studio UI concurrently. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop both. 144: 145: ```bash 146: python -m client.run 147: ``` 148: 149: | Service | URL | 150: |---|---| 151: | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | 152: | The Living Studio UI | http://localhost:8501 | 153: 154: ### 🔧 Manual Split-Terminal (alternative) 155: 156: Open two terminals and run each process separately: 157: 158: ```bash 159: # Terminal 1 — MCP server 160: python -m mcp_server 161: 162: # Terminal 2 — Streamlit chat UI 163: streamlit run client/src/client/app.py 164: ``` 165: 166: ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) 167: 168: To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: 169: 170: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and 171: - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. 172: 173: A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 174: 175: 1. **Install a local LLM server** 176: 177: Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): 178: 179: ```bash 180: pip install llama-cpp-python 181: ``` 182: 183: 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** 184: 185: Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 186: 187: 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** 188: 189: Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Streamlit client (`client/src/client/app.py`): 190: 191: ```bash 192: python -m llama_cpp.server \ 193: --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ 194: --model_alias local-tools-model \ 195: --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ 196: --chat_format openai 197: ``` 198: 199: This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 200: 201: 4. **Configure the Streamlit client** 202: 203: `client/src/client/app.py` reads the following environment variables (with sensible defaults): 204: 205: | Variable | Default | 206: |---|---| 207: | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | 208: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | 209: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | 210: | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | 211: 212: You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Streamlit sidebar under **"LLM Configuration"**. 213: 214: 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** 215: 216: - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: 217: 218: ```bash 219: curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models 220: ``` 221: 222: If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. 223: 224: - Start the MCP server and Streamlit UI (either via `python -m client.run` or the split-terminal commands above). 225: - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: *"Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository."* 226: - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. 227: - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. 228: 229: ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing 230: 231: Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. 232: 233: --- 234: 235: ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) 236: 237: The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. You can mirror them locally with: 238: 239: ```bash 240: # Ruff lint and formatting checks (per-file config comes from each project's pyproject.toml) 241: uv run ruff check . 242: uv run ruff format --check . 243: 244: # Type checking (run per project so each project's config applies) 245: uv run --directory core mypy . 246: uv run --directory mcp_server mypy . 247: uv run --directory local_server mypy . 248: uv run --directory client mypy . 249: uv run --directory cli mypy . 250: uv run --directory connectors mypy . 251: 252: # Security scanning 253: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src 254: 255: # Tests (same as CI) 256: uv run --directory core pytest 257: uv run --directory mcp_server pytest 258: uv run --directory local_server pytest 259: uv run --directory client pytest 260: uv run --directory cli pytest 261: uv run --directory connectors pytest 262: ``` 263: 264: To run these automatically before each commit, enable the bundled pre-commit hooks: 265: 266: ```bash 267: uv tool install pre-commit 268: pre-commit install 269: ``` 270: 271: After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` will run on staged files whenever you commit. You can also trigger them manually with: 272: 273: ```bash 274: pre-commit run --all-files 275: ``` 276: 277: --- 278: 279: ## ✅ Testing 280: 281: Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely in-memory — no running server required. Each project owns its tests. CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and stores a coverage report as a build artifact: 282: 283: ```bash 284: uv run --directory core pytest 285: uv run --directory mcp_server pytest 286: uv run --directory local_server pytest 287: uv run --directory client pytest 288: uv run --directory cli pytest 289: uv run --directory connectors pytest 290: ``` 291: 292: ### 📊 Test Coverage Map 293: 294: | File | What it covers | 295: |---|---| 296: | `core/tests/test_models.py` | Domain models and ODI opportunity-score computation | 297: | `core/tests/test_service.py` | `ODIService` jobs/steps/outcomes and Customer Outcome CRUD | 298: | `mcp_server/tests/test_odi.py` | Full ODI workflow (add job → steps → outcomes → retrieval) + capabilities tool | 299: | `mcp_server/tests/test_customer_outcomes.py` | Customer Outcomes CRUD, filtering, computed opportunity scores, and tool validation | 300: | `mcp_server/tests/test_server_tools.py` | Error handling and retrieval for the MCP tools | 301: | `mcp_server/tests/test_tools.py` | Tool response-shape contract for `add_job` | 302: | `local_server/tests/test_api.py` | Local FastAPI health endpoint | 303: | `client/tests/test_run.py` | Dev launcher helpers (port checks) | 304: | `cli/tests/test_cli.py` | CLI `--version` and `--help` behavior | 305: | `cli/tests/test_outcomes_cli.py` | Customer Outcomes CLI subcommands with MCP stub | 306: | `cli/tests/test_connectors_cli.py` | CLI `connectors` add/list/health/ingest adapter | 307: | `connectors/tests/test_registry.py` | JSON connector registry persist/load and kind checks | 308: | `connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py` | In-memory FastMCP health and ingest records | 309: 310: **Conventions:** 311: 312: - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named `test_*.py`. 313: - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`. 314: - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests. 315: - The server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before each test. 316: 317: > [!TIP] 318: > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the results automatically. 319: 320: ### 🧪 Agent Session Tracking 321: 322: Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview) CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured checkpoints. 323: 324: --- 325: 326: ## 🤝 Superpowers with Pi 327: 328: This project includes [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) as a [Pi package](https://pi.dev/docs/packages). When using [Pi](https://pi.dev) with this project, Superpowers skills and extensions are automatically loaded. 329: 330: To enable: 331: 332: 1. Install Pi: `curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh` 333: 2. Trust the project (first time only): `pi config --local --approve` 334: 3. Start Pi: `pi` 335: 336: The `.pi/settings.json` declares the Superpowers package. Pi will clone it and load: 337: 338: - **Extension**: `superpowers.ts` — injects the `using-superpowers` bootstrap at session startup and after compaction 339: - **Skills**: 12 Superpowers skills (TDD, subagent-driven-development, systematic-debugging, etc.) 340: 341: > [!NOTE] 342: > Superpowers is also available for OpenCode via the plugin in `opencode.json`. The Pi package provides native Pi integration without needing the OpenCode compatibility layer. 343: 344: ### 🧼 Developer Workflow for Formatting 345: 346: - **When editing Python files**, either: 347: - Rely on the **pre-commit hooks** above (recommended), or 348: - Run Ruff formatting directly before pushing: 349: 350: ```bash 351: uv run ruff format . 352: ``` 353: 354: - **CI behavior**: 355: - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files. 356: - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only. 357: - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the changes, and push again. 358: 359: --- 360: 361: ## ☁️ Deployment 362: 363: The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents. 364: 365: ### 🧪 Test Chat (UI) 366: 367: Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser: 368: 369: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)** 370: 371: ### 🔌 MCP Server Endpoint 372: 373: Integrate via the MCP protocol at: 374: 375: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)** 376: 377: > [!IMPORTANT] 378: > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a client. 379: 380: --- 381: 382: ## 🗺️ Roadmap & Next Steps 383: 384: As we validate the feasibility of this architecture, our next milestones include: 385: 386: - [x] **External MCP client connector**: Pluggable connectors package with an HTTP MCP ingest client, CLI adapter, and in-memory tests. 387: - [ ] **Map ingested evidence onto ODI artifacts**: Turn connector records into jobs, outcomes, or evidence without mixing connector plumbing into the ODI store. 388: - [ ] **Additional connector kinds**: REST/webhooks and similar integrations implementing the same `Connector` protocol. 389: - [ ] **ODI Schema Definition**: Define standardized Pydantic models for *Jobs*, *Steps*, and *Outcomes*. 390: - [x] **CLI Dataset Commands**: Extend `cli/` so the ODI dataset can be created, queried, and scored from the terminal, in addition to the current MCP path. 391: - [ ] **Context Tooling**: Replace the dummy `greet` tool with capabilities like `get_job_map(job_id)` or `evaluate_outcome(statement)`. 392: - [ ] **Data Persistence Layer**: Connect the fastmcp server to a lightweight vector or relational database containing actual user research data. 393: - [ ] **Agentic Integration**: Hook the client up to an LLM (e.g., via LangChain or standard OpenAI clients) so the LLM can *discover* the ODI tools and intelligently request customer insights when ideating features. 394: 395: --- 396: 397: ## 🤝 Contributing 398: 399: Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Please ensure any change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) before opening a pull request. 400: 401: --- 402: 403: ## 📄 License 404: 405: No license has been specified for this repository yet. Until one is added, all rights reserved by the maintainers. Please reach out before reuse or redistribution. 406: 407: --- 408: 409:
410: 411: *Let's build AI that builds what people actually need.* 412: 413:

Makes an authenticated HTTP request to the GitHub API and prints the response.

The endpoint argument should either be a path of a GitHub API v3 endpoint, or
`graphql` to access the GitHub API v4.

Placeholder values `{owner}`, `{repo}`, and `{branch}` in the endpoint
argument will get replaced with values from the repository of the current
directory or the repository specified in the `GH_REPO` environment variable.
Note that in some shells, for example PowerShell, you may need to enclose
any value that contains `{...}` in quotes to prevent the shell from
applying special meaning to curly braces.

The `-p/--preview` flag enables opting into previews, which are feature-flagged,
experimental API endpoints or behaviors. The API expects opt-in via the `Accept`
header with format `application/vnd.github.<preview-name>-preview+json` and this
command facilitates that via `--preview <preview-name>`. To send a request for
the corsair and scarlet witch previews, you could use `-p corsair,scarlet-witch`
or `--preview corsair --preview scarlet-witch`.

The default HTTP request method is `GET` normally and `POST` if any parameters
were added. Override the method with `--method`.

Pass one or more `-f/--raw-field` values in `key=value` format to add static string
parameters to the request payload. To add non-string or placeholder-determined values, see
`-F/--field` below. Note that adding request parameters will automatically switch the
request method to `POST`. To send the parameters as a `GET` query string instead, use
`--method GET`.

The `-F/--field` flag has magic type conversion based on the format of the value:

- literal values `true`, `false`, `null`, and integer numbers get converted to
  appropriate JSON types;
- placeholder values `{owner}`, `{repo}`, and `{branch}` get populated with values
  from the repository of the current directory;
- if the value starts with `@`, the rest of the value is interpreted as a
  filename to read the value from. Pass `-` to read from standard input.

For GraphQL requests, all fields other than `query` and `operationName` are
interpreted as GraphQL variables.

To pass nested parameters in the request payload, use `key[subkey]=value` syntax when
declaring fields. To pass nested values as arrays, declare multiple fields with the
syntax `key[]=value1`, `key[]=value2`. To pass an empty array, use `key[]` without a
value.

To pass pre-constructed JSON or payloads in other formats, a request body may be read
from file specified by `--input`. Use `-` to read from standard input. When passing the
request body this way, any parameters specified via field flags are added to the query
string of the endpoint URL.

In `--paginate` mode, all pages of results will sequentially be requested until
there are no more pages of results. For GraphQL requests, this requires that the
original query accepts an `$endCursor: String` variable and that it fetches the
`pageInfo{ hasNextPage, endCursor }` set of fields from a collection. Each page is a separate
JSON array or object. Pass `--slurp` to wrap all pages of JSON arrays or objects
into an outer JSON array.

For more information about output formatting flags, see `gh help formatting`.

USAGE
  gh api <endpoint> [flags]

FLAGS
      --allow-escape-sequences   Allow printing terminal escape sequences
      --cache duration           Cache the response, e.g. "3600s", "60m", "1h"
  -F, --field key=value          Add a typed parameter in key=value format (use "@<path>" or "@-" to read value from file or stdin)
  -H, --header key:value         Add a HTTP request header in key:value format
      --hostname string          The GitHub hostname for the request (default "github.com")
  -i, --include                  Include HTTP response status line and headers in the output
      --input file               The file to use as body for the HTTP request (use "-" to read from standard input)
  -q, --jq string                Query to select values from the response using jq syntax
  -X, --method string            The HTTP method for the request (default "GET")
      --paginate                 Make additional HTTP requests to fetch all pages of results
  -p, --preview strings          Opt into GitHub API previews (names should omit '-preview')
  -f, --raw-field key=value      Add a string parameter in key=value format
      --silent                   Do not print the response body
      --slurp                    Use with "--paginate" to return an array of all pages of either JSON arrays or objects
  -t, --template string          Format JSON output using a Go template; see "gh help formatting"

INHERITED FLAGS

  # Post an issue comment

  # Post nested parameter read from a file
  $ gh api gists -F 'files[myfile.txt][content]=@myfile.txt'
  
  # Add parameters to a GET request
  $ gh api -X GET search/issues -f q='repo:cli/cli is:open remote'
  
  # Use a JSON file as request body

  # Opt into GitHub API previews

  # Print only specific fields from the response
  $ gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues --jq '.[].title'

content.text:
Before planning, seven things I can't determine from the doc or the repo. Grounding notes come from README.md, `.gitignore`, workflow layout, and live checks of the two hosted URLs. Ranked by how much a wrong guess would cost.

---

**1. What exactly should the primary CTA "Try the hosted demo" link to, given that neither hosted entry point is actually tryable by an anonymous visitor?**

I verified both: `https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat` 302-redirects to `auth.horizon.prefect.io` (Horizon/Prefect account sign-in required), and `https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp` returns **401** on initialize. The doc acknowledges "hosted endpoint requires auth" but still designates the hosted demo as *the* single obvious CTA. So I don't know which of these is true: (a) the gated Horizon login is an acceptable CTA target — sign-up is free/frictionless and we just link it; (b) we need an intermediate access/request step designed into the page; or (c) the primary CTA should actually become the local quickstart (`uv sync --all-packages && python -m client.run`), with hosted demoted. This choice determines the hero, the entire conversion flow, and which of the doc's seven sections is the terminal action — it's the single load-bearing decision on the page. Related sub-question I also can't check without credentials: does the hosted instance have representative seeded ODI data, or would a new visitor land in an empty demo?

**2. What channel should the site present for obtaining access, and is publishing that channel approved?**

README says only "reach out to the maintainers." The page needs a concrete, clickable path (GitHub Issues enabled? Discussions? email address? Discord? calendly?). Wrong guess matters twice: no channel = dead-end conversion (violates the "one obvious CTA" goal), and publishing a personal email or a channel that isn't actually monitored is worse than none. This shapes the hero's supporting microcopy, section 6 ("Honest status"), and the footer.

**3. What authentication scheme does the hosted MCP endpoint use — and may the site show it?**

Section 5 ("For builders") wants an MCP endpoint snippet, but nothing in the repo documents the auth mechanism for `agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp` (no bearer/header/env-var convention anywhere in code or docs — the only `API_KEY` reference is the unrelated local LLM key in `client/src/client/app.py`). I can't invent a header name or token-issuance flow for a copy-paste snippet. Options I'd need a ruling on: give me the real scheme; explicitly show local-only config (`http://localhost:8000/mcp`) with a prose note that hosted credentials come from the maintainers; or omit the connection snippet entirely. Different answers change section 5's content and whether it demonstrates value to the "AI/agent developers" audience or just the install one-liner.

**4. Is a committed PNG binary acceptable for the OG/Twitter card, and if so, who generates it — a script run by you, or the deploy workflow?**

The doc offers "committed PNG generated by a tiny script *or* an SVG OG fallback" and doesn't resolve it. Matters because: the repo today contains zero binaries and zero visual assets, so adding one is a precedent; and generating the PNG inside the Pages workflow would violate the stated constraint that sources stay directly deployable via `actions/upload-pages-artifact`. Social share previews are also the main earned-distribution artifact for a marketing site — an SVG-only fallback renders poorly or not at all on X/Slack/LinkedIn/iMessage. I need to know which of: (a) yes, commit a PNG, I'll provide/re-run a generator script; (b) no binaries, SVG fallback and accept degraded cards; or (c) PNG generation is run manually by you at design time as a one-off.

**5. Does the "Honest status / when" section have any real dates or milestones we're allowed to state, or is the intended message explicitly "no committed timeline"?**

Section 6 promises "roadmap framing (when)." The README roadmap has no dates and its checked/unchecked items are themselves partly stale relative to the working tree (e.g., CLI dataset commands marked done, context tooling still open). I can't invent dates, and I shouldn't guess whether the Jobsian "when" answer is a bold timeline or a deliberately humble "experimental, no dates committed." The answer changes whether section 6 is a dated roadmap (needs input I don't have), a curated "what works today / what's next" list mirroring main's README, or a plain honesty disclaimer — a different amount and kind of copy, with different risk profiles for over-promising on an experimental product.

**6. Must the Living Studio illustrative mock correspond to the actual shipped Streamlit UI, or may it be a stylized abstraction?**

The doc rules out a fake screenshot but doesn't set the fidelity bar. The real app (`client/src/client/app.py`) advertises specific surfaces — Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, Impact Simulation, Causal Lineage, conversational agent. A wide-fidelity mock risks depicting capabilities that don't exist yet on a page whose entire thesis is "no guesses"; an abstraction risks a pretty picture that tells the reader nothing. Wrong guess in either direction undercuts the credibility the page is built on, and the two answers imply very different amounts of investigation into `app.py` before designing the SVG/CSS.

**7. What is the approved citation target for the ~86% ODI success-rate claim?**

The doc says cite "carefully ... as reported by Strategyn/ODI literature" but not *what* we link to. The obvious in-repo source, `knowledge/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf`, is third-party copyrighted material sitting in a public no-license repo — hotlinking it from a marketing page raises the profile of a redistribution that's arguably already questionable. Alternatives are plain-text attribution ("as reported in ODI/Strategyn literature") with no link, or linking to Strategyn's own public pages. This changes the markup of the one stat callout on the page, and it's a legal-adjacent call I shouldn't make unilaterally.
